issues.legal_issue: Land acquisition proceedings must be completed within a reasonable time, and unjustified prolonged delay in making awards may require additional compensation when the statutory valuation date would otherwise leave owners with substantially outdated market value.
material_facts: Declarations had been made, but awards were not made for many years afterward; awards were made only between 1980 and 1983.
The authorities gave no adequate explanation for failing to make any awards until 1980, including after the dismissal of challenges to the acquisition proceedings.
Compensation was calculated by reference to market value on the dates of the acquisition notifications, which substantially predated the awards.
The affected owners were small cultivators, and the delay occurred after the earlier challenges to the acquisitions had been resolved.
issues.conclusion: The delay in making the awards was unreasonable and unjustified. Rather than quash the acquisitions, the Court directed payment of additional compensation calculated at 12 per cent per annum on the market value at the notification dates, for the period beginning two years after the earlier judgment resolving the challenges and ending when the awards were made.
issues.legal_principle: Where a statute confers a power without prescribing a time limit, it must be exercised within a reasonable time; what is reasonable depends on the circumstances and nature of the power. State of Gujarat v. Patel Raghav Natha and Mansaram v. S.P. Pathak apply that principle. The Land Acquisition Act’s scheme contemplates expeditious completion of acquisition, and State of M.P. v. Vishnu Prasad Sharma, Ambalal Purshottam v. Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation and Khadim Hussain v. State of U.P. support the requirement that acquisition proceedings proceed without unreasonable delay. Sections 11 and 23 fix market value by reference to the Section 4 notification date, while the second proviso to Article 31-A requires compensation not below market value. On these facts, the unexplained delay frustrated the statutory and constitutional compensation requirements and warranted additional compensation.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and declarations_issued and awards_delayed_for_many_years and obstacle_to_award_completion_removed and no_adequate_explanation and compensation_based_on_substantially_older_market_value

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerned the compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.declarations_issued: The acquiring authority had formally declared that the land was required for acquisition.
predicates.awards_delayed_for_many_years: The authority took many years after the declarations to make the compensation awards.
predicates.obstacle_to_award_completion_removed: Earlier legal challenges that could have impeded completion of the acquisitions had been resolved.
predicates.no_adequate_explanation: The acquiring authority did not adequately explain its prolonged failure to make the awards.
predicates.compensation_based_on_substantially_olde: The compensation was assessed using a market value date substantially earlier than the date of the awards.

issues.definition: When an acquisition proceeding remains without awards for many years after the declarations and impediments to completion have been removed, with no adequate explanation and compensation based on substantially older market value, additional compensation may be awarded for the delay.

issues.legal_issue: The transitional provision prescribing a deadline for awards does not validate or excuse unreasonable delay that occurred before it took effect.
material_facts: The declarations had been published before the 1984 amendment took effect.
The awards in these proceedings had been made before that amendment took effect.
The authorities relied on the amendment’s transitional deadline to argue that the earlier delay was permissible.
issues.conclusion: The transitional provision did not validate or justify the authorities’ earlier inaction, and it did not apply to proceedings in which awards had already been made before the amendment came into force.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act imposes a deadline for making an award and provides for lapse if the deadline is not met. Its proviso gives a deadline for awards following declarations published before the amendment commenced; it does not retrospectively validate prior delay or condone inaction that had already occurred. A proviso carves out an exception within the provision rather than supplying retrospective validation.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerned the compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.pre_amendment_declaration: The declaration that the land was required for acquisition was published before the new award-deadline rule took effect.
predicates.award_made_before_deadline_provision_too: The compensation award was made before the new award-deadline rule took effect.
predicates.authority_claims_prior_delay_was_validat: The acquiring authority argued that the new deadline rule excused or validated its earlier delay.

issues.definition: If an acquisition declaration predates a new award-deadline rule, the award was already made before that rule took effect, and the authority relies on the rule to excuse earlier delay, the earlier delay is not thereby validated.

issues.legal_issue: When quashing a delayed acquisition would harm overriding public interests and affect developed land or third parties, a court may deny quashing while granting modified relief for the injury caused by official inaction.
material_facts: The owners sought to quash acquisition proceedings after substantial delay, having waited many years to challenge the proceedings on that basis.

By the time relief was considered, the acquiring authorities had taken possession of much of the land and development had occurred, including use of the land to provide shelter and implement a planned city.
Third-party interests had arisen and the affected third parties were not before the Court.
The authorities had failed to justify their delay, leaving the owners injured by the prolonged inaction.
issues.conclusion: Quashing the acquisitions was inappropriate because of the public interest, development and intervening third-party interests. The Court instead granted modified relief by directing additional compensation; the owners’ delay in seeking relief did not excuse the authorities’ failure to perform their duties within a reasonable time.
issues.legal_principle: Delay by a claimant in invoking writ jurisdiction must be considered together with the statutory authority’s own inaction; claimant delay does not make the authority’s failure immaterial. Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi and Ramjas Foundation v. Union of India recognize the relevance of claimant delay in challenges to acquisition proceedings. Where land has been taken and developed for public purposes and third-party interests have arisen, quashing may be inappropriate, but a court may grant modified relief under Articles 226 or 32 of the Constitution to address the injury caused by official delay.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_land_acquisition and authority_unreasonably_delayed_proceedings and land_taken_or_developed_for_public_use and third_party_interests_affected and quashing_would_harm_public_interest

predicates.writ_challenge_to_land_acquisition: An owner sought writ relief against a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.authority_unreasonably_delayed_proceedin: The acquiring authority failed to complete the proceedings within a reasonable time.
predicates.land_taken_or_developed_for_public_use: The authority had taken the land or it had been developed or used for a public purpose.
predicates.third_party_interests_affected: Interests of people who were not before the court had arisen in the land.
predicates.quashing_would_harm_public_interest: Setting aside the acquisition would adversely affect public interests served by the land’s use.

issues.definition: Where an authority unreasonably delays an acquisition but the land has been taken or developed for public use, third-party interests are affected, and quashing would harm the public interest, the court may deny quashing and grant modified compensation relief.
